description: Content Service operational dashboard — saturation, latency breakdown, failure modes. Drives load-test reads.

panels.description: Concurrent in-flight Fetch calls. Compare against GLOBAL_MAX_INFLIGHT (default 200) — when this gauge plateaus there, requests start queueing in the semaphore and queue time shows up as request latency.
panels.title: In-flight requests (global vs stream)

panels.description: Request rate split by status. Sustained 'failed' is the load-test failure signal.
panels.title: Request rate by status

panels.description: End-to-end Fetch latency p50/p95/p99 across all api+content_type combinations.
panels.title: Request latency (p50/p95/p99)

panels.description: Rejections by reason. Non-zero = you've hit a concurrency ceiling. reason ∈ {global_full, stream_full, shutdown}.
panels.title: Rejections by reason

panels.description: Cache S3 op latency p99 split by op. Separates S3 latency from CS code paths. NOTE: since 2026-08 the read path serves hits HEAD-only (bodies are delivered via CacheLocation), so expect `get` volume to be a small fraction of `head` — a rising get rate means the extraction path or sha safety-net is doing the reading.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, bucket, op) (rate(content_cache_op_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="$namespace", job="$job"}[1m])))

panels.title: Cache op p99 latency (by bucket/op)

panels.description: NATS fetch outcomes per second by connector. outcome ∈ {completed, pickup_timeout, worker_timeout, canceled, error}. The *_timeout series are the load-test failure signals — non-zero pickup_timeout means connectors aren't keeping up; worker_timeout means they're stuck mid-fetch.
panels.title: NATS fetch outcomes by connector

panels.description: Cache hit ratio by bucket. Drop under load = colder cache or churn.

targets.expr: sum by (bucket) (rate(content_cache_hits_total{namespace="$namespace", job="$job"}[1m])) / (sum by (bucket) (rate(content_cache_hits_total{namespace="$namespace", job="$job"}[1m])) + sum by (bucket) (rate(content_cache_misses_total{namespace="$namespace", job="$job"}[1m])))

panels.title: Cache hit ratio (by bucket)

panels.description: Text extraction p99 latency split by outcome. Only `success`/`failed` populate the histogram (skipped/breaker_open record duration=0 by design).
panels.title: Extraction p99 latency (by status)

panels.description: NATS two-phase reply latency p99 by connector. pickup = publish → PROCESSING signal; worker = PROCESSING → COMPLETED reply. PICKUP_TIMEOUT and WORKER_TIMEOUT both default to 30s — sustained p99 climbing toward those thresholds means timeouts are imminent. Pairs with the NATS-outcomes panel.
panels.title: NATS two-phase reply p99 (by connector)

panels.description: Cache write latency p50/p95/p99, SUCCESS ONLY — canceled/timeout are definitionally long-running (they measure how long a transfer ran before being abandoned) and poison the percentiles when mixed in; they have their own panel. Duration covers stream ingest + S3 upload but EXCLUDES the sha256 stamp copy (own panel). Buckets are explicit since 2026-08 — percentiles before that deploy were interpolation artifacts of the SDK's millisecond-scale defaults and read ~10-1000x too high.
panels.title: Cache write latency — success only (p50/p95/p99)

panels.description:
DISABLED — pending future work. content-service does not emit `content_extraction_circuit_state`, so this panel shows No data; there is no extractor circuit breaker in the service today. It is a placeholder for the breaker described in the xberg backpressure work, and will start working unchanged if that lands (the breaker is specified to report 0=closed / 1=half-open / 2=open, which the value mappings below already expect).

Until then, use `Retry attempts by error code` for extractor-saturation signal: a rising SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE line is xberg answering 503, which is what a breaker would trip on.
panels.title: Extractor circuit (DISABLED — pending breaker)

panels.description: S3 cache operation errors per second. error_type ∈ {read_failed, write_failed, other}.
panels.title: Cache op errors (by error_type)

panels.description: Cache write outcomes from S3Store. result ∈ {success, read_error, size_mismatch, s3_error, canceled, timeout}. `timeout` = the CACHE_WRITE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS bound fired (was folded into `canceled` before 2026-08); `size_mismatch` now also deletes the truncated object.
panels.title: Cache write outcomes

panels.description: Requests FAILED during graceful shutdown drain. Should be zero except during deploy/restart.
panels.title: Shutdown-time failures

panels.description: sha256 safety-net activations — fires when the raw object carries no sha256 user-metadata (the stamp is written synchronously at cache-write time, so this should be ~zero outside legacy objects aging out of the 7d raw TTL). Steady non-zero `computed_in_process` = stamping regression; `raw_head_miss_text_hit` = text served after its raw was evicted AND the text object predates the sha stamp.
panels.title: sha256 safety-net activations

panels.description: Text extraction outcomes per second. status ∈ {success, failed, skipped, breaker_open}. Sustained `breaker_open` = kreuzberg is sick; `skipped` rate spikes when files exceed EXTRACTION_MAX_SIZE.
panels.title: Extraction outcomes

panels.description: Distribution of bytes written per S3 cache Put — p50/p95/p99. Bodies above the transfer manager's 16 MiB multipart threshold take the multipart path. Useful for sizing payload-mix in load tests. 5m window deliberately wider than other panels — write events are infrequent and benefit from smoothing. Buckets are explicit (4KiB–5GiB) since 2026-08; earlier data used millisecond-scale defaults and is unreadable.
panels.title: Cache write size distribution

panels.description: Attribution of successful cache-write time: `stream-wait` is the portion spent blocked reading the connector's upload stream (paced by the connector pulling from Box/SharePoint/etc.), so `total − stream-wait ≈ S3-side time`. A slow write with high stream-wait is a slow SOURCE, not a slow cache — this is the split that makes 'cache write latency' actionable.
panels.title: Cache write: total vs connector stream-wait (p95, success)

panels.description: How long abandoned transfers ran before dying. `canceled` = the peer went away (connector crash, pod eviction, client deadline); `timeout` = the CACHE_WRITE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS bound fired. These are definitionally the long tail — kept OUT of the main latency panel so they can be read as what they are: client-abandonment behavior, not cache performance.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, result) (rate(content_cache_write_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", result=~"canceled|timeout"}[5m])))

panels.title: Cache write — abandoned transfers (canceled/timeout)

panels.description: The post-upload sha256 metadata stamp (a server-side CopyObject self-copy, synchronous within Put but excluded from write-duration). Cost scales with object size — the copy rewrites the whole object, up to the 5GB CopyObject ceiling. Sustained `error` = objects left unstamped → sha safety-net activations downstream.
panels.title: sha256 stamp (CopyObject) p95 by result

panels.description: Cache writes where the connector declared no size, so the post-upload byte-count validation was skipped — a client stream that died with a clean half-close mid-body is indistinguishable from a complete upload for these. Should be ~zero; any sustained rate means a connector is uploading unverifiable (possibly truncated) content.
panels.title: Unverified writes (no declared size)

panels.description: Upload streams currently admitted on the transfer listener. Each in-flight multipart upload holds ~48-64MiB of transfer-manager buffers; the uploadAdmission interceptor caps this service-wide at UPLOAD_MAX_CONCURRENT (default 32 — the red line). Sustained saturation = connectors are queueing behind the gate.
panels.title: Upload streams in flight (cap 32)
Retry amplification — how one connector error becomes a platform stall (NXE-2480)

panels.description: Connector fetches issued per document actually drained by the privacy pipeline. 1.0 = healthy: every document fetched exactly once. The retry ladder is extractRetryMaxAttempts (5) × JetStream MaxDeliver (3) = 15, so a value approaching 15 means every failing document is consuming the whole ladder while holding one of the caller's workers. Measured 14.99 throughout the 2026-07-27 outage. NOTE: pii_* is emitted by the privacy job, so this reads true only while a privacy scan is running.
panels.title: Fetch amplification (fetches per document)

panels.description:
`failed_budget` is the one to read first — it is the common outcome now. The caller-wait budget (CALLER_WAIT_BUDGET_SECONDS, 5s) stops the in-handler retry ladder early, REPLIES to the caller so its worker is released, then Nak's with a 30s delay so the document is still retried. It was previously absent from this panel's query, which hid the majority of retry activity.

`failed` is a mixed bag: the two silent-Nak paths (in-handler attempts exhausted with deliveries left, and the request deadline firing) send NO reply, but a malformed request and a non-retryable manager failure also land here and DO reply. Treat a rising `failed` as "documents are being retried", not as "callers are stranded".

`failed_terminal` is the only outcome that both replies and Ack's — either MaxDeliver was reached or the budget was spent on the last allowed delivery. It is the end of the line for that document in this scan.

All three were EXACTLY 0.00/s during a clean S3-only window running at 87 completed/s, and ran sustained through the 2026-07-27 incident.
panels.title: Retry outcomes — failed vs budget vs terminal

panels.description: Requests slower than the histogram's top bucket. The service permits pickup 60s + worker 180s = 240s but content_request_duration_seconds stops at 60s, so p99 is extrapolated and UNDERSTATES the tail — count the overflow directly instead. During the 2026-07-27 outage p95 pinned at exactly 29.00s for 360 consecutive samples, the interpolation signature of 100% of requests sitting in the (10s, 30s] bucket. NOTE the bucket label is decimal-formatted: le="60.0". Querying le="60" returns nothing.

targets.expr: sum(rate(content_request_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", api="nats", le="+Inf"}[5m])) - sum(rate(content_request_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", api="nats", le="60.0"}[5m]))

panels.title: Requests past the 60s top bucket

panels.description: Privacy document throughput against the rate below which its OpenSearch Point-in-Time lease expires. The reader paginates only as documents drain, and its consumers synchronise, so the gap between searches is 32 consumers × 1000-document pages ÷ throughput. Against a 30-minute lease that gives a critical rate of 32000/1800 = 17.8 docs/s. Sustained operation below the red line ends in a 404 search_context_missing_exception — and because the reader error is discarded at main.go:219, the scan then reports SUCCESS having read only part of the index. Requires a running privacy scan.
panels.title: Privacy throughput vs the PIT critical rate

panels.description:
Time a request spent waiting for an extraction slot before reaching xberg. This is the panel that separates "we queued" from "xberg was slow on this file" — without it both surface as the same error codes. Rising p95 here with `Extraction slots in use` pinned at capacity is a queueing problem, not a document problem. Buckets run to 600s because the extraction semaphore has no acquire timeout.

Split by lane, because that is the question the gate exists to answer. EXTRACTION_PRIORITY_MAX_CONSECUTIVE is wired so interactive extractions are not starved by pipeline ones, and undimensioned this panel shows the queue is deep without saying whether the requests waiting are the ones a human is waiting on. `interactive` climbing toward `bulk` means the priority lane is no longer buying anything.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, lane) (rate(content_extraction_queue_wait_seconds_bucket{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", outcome="admitted"}[5m])))
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, lane) (rate(content_extraction_queue_wait_seconds_bucket{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", outcome="admitted"}[5m])))
histogram_quantile(0.50, sum by (le, lane) (rate(content_extraction_queue_wait_seconds_bucket{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", outcome="admitted"}[5m])))

panels.title: Extraction queue wait (admitted)

panels.description:
Occupancy of the extraction gate against EXTRACTION_MAX_CONCURRENCY (60 — the red line). That 60 is the DEPLOYED value, set under `contentService.env` in the applications chart; the code default is 10, so re-check the red line if dev retunes it. Occupancy SATURATES: once it is pinned it cannot tell you how far behind you are, which is what the queue-wait panel is for. `aborted/s` is requests whose deadline expired while queueing — sustained non-zero means the gate is shedding work rather than pacing it.

The total is kept as its own series because the red line applies to it, not to either lane alone. The per-lane split is what tells you who is holding the gate: `bulk` filling it during a scan is expected, but interactive extractions should still get in — read alongside `Extraction queue wait`, and note that slots held by extractions whose caller already left are counted in `Extractions that outlived their caller`.
panels.title: Extraction slots in use (cap 60) + abandoned waits

panels.description: In-handler retry attempts, by the extraction/content error code that caused them. This is the amplification signal: a busy extractor answers 503 (SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE), which is retryable and earns roughly three attempts per delivery across three deliveries — so the code meaning "stop sending me work" is the one that generates the most. TIMEOUT is deliberately capped lower. A rising SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE line during an incident is content-service making the backlog worse.
panels.title: Retry attempts by error code

panels.description: Fetch failures by the connector's own error code, which is the pivot from an error spike back to the URNs that caused it — the contentpb taxonomy collapses most connector codes onto INTERNAL, so `code` alone cannot say why. `retryable` splits "will be tried again" from terminal. CONNECTOR_UNAVAILABLE means no connector answered our reply inbox within PICKUP_TIMEOUT_SECONDS; it does NOT mean the request was lost — it stays queued on CONTENT_FETCH.
panels.title: Connector fetch errors by code

panels.description:
Valkey claims taken before a connector fetch or an xberg extraction, so two replicas don't do the same work. Expect everything but `won` to sit at zero until KEDA scales past one replica.

`won` — this pod took the claim and is doing the work.
`lost` — another replica holds it, so this one waits for the output instead.
`preempted` — interactive work took a bulk holder's claim. A DELIBERATE duplicate: the displaced holder keeps working, so for a window two replicas do the same work. That is the price of putting a human ahead of a scan, and it is a separate label so the price is visible rather than folded into `won`.
`held_by_self` — this pod found its OWN earlier claim, almost always a fetch claim retained past a reply timeout. No peer is involved and the work is at a connector. Split out of `lost` on purpose: counted as a cross-pod loss, a connector slowdown on one pod read as a dedup success story.
`duplicated` — gave up waiting and did the work anyway knowing a peer holds the claim. Only interactive requests do this, because a synchronous call has no redelivery to defer to. Buys a full duplicate.
`lease_lost` — a renewal found the claim gone while the work was still running: it lapsed, or an interactive claimant preempted it. This is the LEADING INDICATOR of duplicate work.
`unavailable` — Valkey is unreachable and dedup has silently degraded. Everything still works, it just costs duplicate fetches and extractions.
`disabled` — dedup is not running at all for that phase: VALKEY_HOST unset, or that phase's marker TTL zeroed. Emitted deliberately so "dedup is off" is visible; an absent series looks identical to no traffic. With both TTLs set and Valkey wired, this should be flat zero.

The two worth watching are `disabled` (off by configuration, a likelier regression than an outage) and `lease_lost` (duplicate work is now happening).
panels.title: Cross-pod dedup — claim outcomes

panels.description:
Outcome of waiting for output another worker is producing, split by who we are waiting on. `peer` is dedup working: another replica holds the claim, so a `peer`/`satisfied` is a connector fetch or xberg run that did NOT happen twice. `connector` is NOT dedup: we hold the claim ourselves and our own reply timeout fired, so those count connector slowness — reading them as dedup overstates the payoff by exactly the number of reply timeouts. The two move for different reasons: `peer` rises with replica count and hot keys, `connector` with source-system load. phase=extract is always `peer`, since an extraction is synchronous and has no dispatched request that could outlive our timeout. Non-`satisfied` outcomes mean this request did the work itself, which is correct behaviour — the wait can only save effort, never cause a failure. `skipped` means there was no deadline left to wait within (PEER_WAIT_SECONDS bounds a peer wait and CONNECTOR_WAIT_SECONDS a connector one, but GET_CONTENT_DEADLINE_SECONDS caps both), so a high `skipped` with a flat `satisfied` is a timing problem, not a dedup problem.

`took_over` is the one to read carefully: the holder stopped renewing its claim with nothing written, so it died, and this request claimed the work and did it itself. In wall-clock terms it looks identical to `expired` and means the opposite — `expired` is "someone is still working and we gave up", `took_over` is "nobody was working and we found out". A steady trickle is pods being recycled mid-fetch; a spike means replicas are dying under load.
panels.title: Cross-pod dedup — work avoided vs redone

panels.description:
How long a wait took before it paid off, split by who we waited on. Filtered to outcome="satisfied" on purpose: an expired wait always equals its whole budget, so including it would flatten every quantile onto the ceiling and say nothing. Which budget depends on who we waited on — PEER_WAIT_SECONDS bounds a peer wait, CONNECTOR_WAIT_SECONDS a connector one, and GET_CONTENT_DEADLINE_SECONDS caps both. They are the same number in dev today only because PEER_WAIT_SECONDS is not templated into the configmap and inherits the connector value. Read with `Cross-pod dedup — work avoided vs redone`, which gives the counts these durations belong to.

`fetch/peer` is how long a follower waits for the replica holding the claim — it tracks connector latency plus whatever was left of the holder's lease when we joined. `fetch/connector` is how far past our own reply timeout the connector actually ran, which is the number to size PICKUP_TIMEOUT_SECONDS and the worker timeout against. `extract/peer` is how long another replica's xberg run took to land.

p50 and p95 only, since splitting by phase and source already yields three series per quantile. Buckets run to 600s (cacheWriteBuckets), so waits longer than that are unresolvable — but the wait budget is well under it, so that ceiling should never bind.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, phase, source) (rate(content_dedup_wait_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", outcome="satisfied"}[5m])))
histogram_quantile(0.50, sum by (le, phase, source) (rate(content_dedup_wait_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="$namespace", job="$job", outcome="satisfied"}[5m])))

panels.title: Cross-pod dedup — how long a paying wait took

panels.description:
Extractions that finished after the caller had already gone. This is DELIBERATE, not a leak: cancelling a POST to xberg mid-flight throws the whole run away, because nothing is persisted until the extractor returns. Carrying on means the caller's retry finds the text cached and pays for a HEAD instead of a second full run.

What it costs is an extraction slot held for work nobody is waiting on, which is why it is counted here rather than left to be inferred from queue depth. Read it against `Extraction slots in use`: a rising count while the gate is pinned means part of your capacity is committed to callers who have left, and the queue behind it is waiting on them.

A steady low rate is the design working — bulk requests hit their delivery deadline and retry into the cache. Sustained `interactive` is worse than sustained `bulk`: a human gave up waiting, and the deadline is doing the abandoning rather than the extractor being slow, so check GET_CONTENT_DEADLINE_SECONDS against the extraction phase before tuning anything else.
panels.title: Extractions that outlived their caller
